newsitem.title: SPAIN: Economic recovery seen delaying Bank of Spain cuts.
newsitem.headline: Economic recovery seen delaying Bank of Spain cuts.

text.p: The Bank of Spain left its key rate steady on Tuesday, disappointing some dealers and highlighting the conflict between a buoyant economy and the need for rates to converge towards those in Germany, analysts said.
Now divided on when the Bank of Spain will use the room it has for further monetary easing, analysts said they will closely track any evidence of possible overheating of the economy.

Focus will move first to Wednesday's announcement of first quarter gross domestic product from the National Statistics Institute INE, then to other data as dealers look for more evidence on the extent and nature of the economic recovery.

"As (European economic and monetary union) gets closer, the Bank of Spain faces a conflict. From one side it wants its 5.25 percent rate to converge steadily toward its German counterpart at 3.0 percent," said Francesco Giordano, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.

"But from the other side the domestic economy is going through a mini-boom and does not need further easing," he said, adding that the most likely thing now was for the monetary authority to wait and see.
The Bank of Spain, which started the current easing cycle in December 1995, has had an aggressive stance with four reductions making a full point off its key rate so far this year.

After May's Consumer Price Index (CPI) showed a yearly increase of 1.5 percent, a 30-year low, from 1.7 percent in April, some analysts forecast that the fifth official rate cut would emerge as soon as this month.
But from now on, the Bank of Spain also admitted that Spanish CPI is likely to pick up.
Earlier on Tuesday, the Bank of Spain forecast in its yearly report a modest pick-up in inflation which is expected to remain "below two percent in the remaining part of the year".
A Reuter poll conducted on Friday showed divided opinions on the possibility of a move today. But on Monday the market seemed to have shifted towards expectations of no change.

Clear signals of economic recovery, such as wage inflation currently running in excess of the CPI and an impressive jump in the April industrial production index, suggested the Bank of Spain could slow down its enthusiasm in cutting rates.
Spanish wage inflation rose 4.2 percent year-on-year in the first quarter.
April industrial production rose 17.7 percent year-on-year versus a 0.2 fall in March, with the less volatile calendar- adjusted data up 12.5 percent versus 4.0 percent one month before.
"The recovery of the Spanish economy is clear. We are at a critical point in the expansion cycle of domestic demand" said Felix Gonzalez, director of Beta Capital in Madrid.
"Now we have to see that the Spanish economy's convergence is sustainable," he added.

After a dramatic fall, inflation is expected to pick up slightly at least, for a less favourable comparison with the year-ago period, as during 1996 CPI rose in the first half and fell in the second half, economists said. "In my opinion, the Bank of Spain has opted for a cautious stance until it could verify that the expected pick-up in CPI was really in line with expectations and until the national statistics institute INE announces quarterly economic growth data," said Elena Pagola at Analistas Financieros Internacionales in Madrid.
Although there was no consensus on the timing of the next rate cut, some analysts suggested that the central bank could decide to wait until the autumn.
"Now the most likely outlook is that it will cut its rate in September or October, when the 1998 budget is ready," said Beta's Gonzalez.

In the meantime, the Bank of Spain will have time to check that wage inflation is on track, allowing CPI to stay below two percent. It will also allow it to make sure the state budget will not boost price pressures, a statement from Banco Central Hispano's research department added.
